orders.rationale: Both answers are accurate. A is correct but brief: it gives the July 2 vote, the July 4 declaration and the 1783 Treaty of Paris. B correctly adds the August 2 signing and the Constitution timeline (1787 adoption, 1788 ratification, government starting in 1789). That separates when the nation began from when the current government began. B's Treaty of Paris line has no citation, a minor gap.

Both are accurate. A is more complete: it adds the start of signing on August 2, the 1787 Constitution, its 1788 ratification and the 1789 start of the federal government, which helps define "created." It also cites sources for most claims. B is correct and concise, mentioning the July 2 vote, but it omits the Constitution and lists sources it never cites.

B is better. It gives correct durations for each reading: about 500 years for the West, about 1,480 years with the East, and about 2,200 years counting from 753 BC. A never states a length. It also wrongly calls 17 January 395 the empire's formal dissolution, when that date marks Theodosius's death and the East–West split.

A correctly gives the start, the Western (476) and Eastern (1453) ends, the durations in years (~500, ~1,480) and the 753 BC context. B never states a length in years. It also wrongly calls 17 January 395 a formal 'dissolution' (Theodosius I died then and the empire split), and its claim that the classical period ended in 380 is questionable.

Answer A contradicts itself: it lists Joseph B. Strauss among the "other experts" besides Strauss. It also leaves out Ellis and Morrow, so it misses the team nature of the design. Answer B gets the key contributors right: Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis (fired in 1931, recognized in 2007), Morrow and Paine. Its build dates and color detail are also correct and supported by its sources.

A is accurate and complete: it credits Strauss, Moisseiff, Ellis (fired 1931, recognized 2007), Morrow and Paine, and gets the 1933–37 dates right. B calls Strauss the primary designer, which overstates his role. It also lists "Joseph B. Strauss" as a separate contributor when that is the same man, and it leaves out Ellis and Morrow.

A wrongly calls Leitch's 1861 idea the earliest rocket concept (rockets date to medieval China), its timeline is muddled, and it skips crewed flight. B's facts are right: Goddard in 1926, the V-2 reaching space in 1944, and Vostok 1 with Gagarin and Korolev. B also answers each meaning of "rocket ship" clearly.

A is accurate and covers the main meanings of "rocket ship" (Goddard 1926, V-2 reaching space, Vostok 1 with Gagarin and Korolev). B wrongly calls Leitch's 1861 idea the earliest rocket concept, ignores the Chinese origins, lists examples out of order, and cites an unused novel. A is clearer and more correct.

A's dates are right, but it barely answers the question. Its one line on goals says the revolution aimed to overthrow the monarchy, which is misleading: the early goal was a constitutional monarchy. B is accurate and nuanced. It covers the Ancien Régime, Enlightenment ideas, the motto, and how the goals changed over time, and its claims match its sources.

A is accurate and nuanced: it explains how the goals changed from constitutional monarchy to a republic, and its claims are backed by its sources. B is thin and oversimplifies. It says the aim was to overthrow the monarchy from the start, which ignores the early constitutional-monarchy phase. It also lists sources it never cites, including one on the 1848 revolution.

B is better. It explains the Lorentz force, why a DC motor needs a commutator and brushes, and how brushless and induction motors differ, all correctly. It also states its assumption that the user means an electric motor. A is accurate but shallow, skips the mechanism, and lists a source it never uses.

A gives an accurate explanation of the Lorentz force, how the commutator works, and how brushless and induction motors differ, and it notes the combustion-engine reading. B is correct but thin. It runs the electric and combustion explanations together and barely explains how the motor keeps turning. It also lists source [2] without citing it anywhere.

B is accurate. It explains the full workflow: model, slicer, then layer-by-layer printing. It also covers the main technologies (FDM, SLA, SLS) with sources that match its claims. A is correct but thin. It never explains how layers are actually made, relies on a dated 2019 claim, and repeats itself.

A gives an accurate explanation of the full workflow: CAD model, then slicer, then building layer by layer. It also explains how FDM, SLA and SLS each make a layer, with relevant sources. B is correct but thin, gives no detail on how the printer works, and uses a dated "as of 2019" claim. A is clearly better.

B explains why planes are fast: thrust against drag, wings carrying the weight, thin air at altitude, a streamlined shape, and why airliners stay below the speed of sound. Its figures are accurate. A barely explains the mechanism, drifts into how the controls feel, cites the X-43 without context and leaves source [2] unused. B is clearer and more useful.

A correctly explains why planes are fast: engine thrust, wings providing lift, thrust balancing drag, thin air at cruise altitude, and the drag rise near the speed of sound. Its figures are accurate. B barely explains why. It wrongly says control response lags more at high speed (response is quicker at speed). The control-feel paragraph is mostly off-topic.

B covers how government arose (Neolithic surpluses, Sumer) and who first theorised it (Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes), accurately and with sources. A rightly says there was no single creator but skips ancient origins and suggests Enlightenment thinkers shaped the concept. Its Montesquieu claim is vague. B is more complete and more useful.

A is better. It explains that government developed gradually after the Neolithic Revolution, gives Sumer as an early example, and names Plato and Aristotle as early theorists, all backed by its sources. B jumps straight to Hobbes, Locke and other later thinkers, skips the ancient origins, and implies the idea came from them. Some of its claims are vague, and it lists source [1] without ever using it.

B is accurate and covers the key differences: founder, the Vedas, atman vs anatta, Brahman/God, and caste. It is also clearly organised. A has correct facts but is shallow. Its conversion comparison doesn't actually contrast the two, it pads with follower counts and leaves out the Vedas rejection and caste.

A is accurate and covers the main differences: founder, the Vedas, atman vs anatta, Brahman/God and caste. It also says a short comparison simplifies things. B gets the self/soul point right but skips the founder, the Vedas and caste. Its shared-deities claim is misleading, and its follower counts add little.

Both answers are accurate. A gets the core difference right but leaves out double-acting powder, how to substitute, and what goes wrong when you swap them. It also lists sources [4]-[7] without citing them. B adds double-acting powder, a worked ratio for using both, and the soapy taste from excess soda. It stays clear and practical, so B is better.

Both are accurate. A also covers double-acting powder, recipes that use both leaveners (with an example) and why you can't swap them. The sources support its claims; the one uncited point (soapy taste) is true. B is correct but only gives the basic distinction, with no double-acting or substitution guidance. A is more complete and more useful.

Both answers correctly say the Mongol Empire was bigger. A gives Rome an oddly exact 5,957,000 km² that doesn't match the usual ~5 million km² estimate, and its sources are vague duplicates. B gives the standard figures (24M vs ~5M km²), adds useful context like populations, Trajan's peak and the British Empire comparison, and cites specific sources.

A is better. Both are correct on the main point, but A also dates the peaks (Trajan in AD 117, the late 13th century for the Mongols), gives populations and notes how long Rome lasted. Its 12,000 km span looks too big, a minor slip. B is correct but thin and has no dates. Its 5,957,000 km² for Rome is a nonstandard figure, and its sources are vague.

Both answers say espresso has more caffeine per ounce and drip coffee has more per serving. B gives per-ounce figures, a range of cup sizes and a double-shot comparison, and it warns that the numbers are averages. A is accurate but thinner: its 80 mg figure for drip is on the low side, and it skips the double shot. B is more complete and more useful.

Both answers say espresso has more caffeine per ounce but less per serving. A gives fuller, accurate numbers (shot, 8-oz and 12-oz cups, double shot) and notes the figures are averages. B is correct, but its 80 mg for a cup of drip is on the low side, it lists source [5] without citing it, and it is less complete.

A wrongly presents AGDLP, an Active Directory group-nesting practice, as Windows' file permission model. It never mentions NTFS ACLs, its static-vs-dynamic contrast is misleading, and its sources look questionable. B accurately covers rwx permissions, the special bits, ACL entries, deny rules, inheritance, auditing, and the difference between no ACL and an empty one, and it notes POSIX ACLs on Linux.

Answer A is accurate. It explains owner/group/other rwx, the special bits, NTFS ACLs with allow/deny entries, inheritance, auditing, the null vs. empty DACL case, and POSIX ACLs. Answer B is misleading: it calls AGDLP, a group-nesting practice for Active Directory, Windows' permission system, and its "static vs. dynamic" contrast is wrong. Its sources are vague and it leaves a lot out.

A's 'technology' answer is circular (AI founded on AI); only Dartmouth 1956 is useful. B correctly names the programmable digital computer and gives accurate Dartmouth details (organizers, McCarthy coining the term in 1955, Logic Theorist), all supported by its sources and clearly explained.

A correctly names the programmable digital computer and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, with accurate details about the organizers and the Logic Theorist, and it notes that the idea of thinking machines is older. B's answer is circular: it says the technology behind AI is AI itself. It gets Dartmouth right but gives nothing else.

Both answers correctly say the Danube flows through Budapest and into the Black Sea. B's extra facts check out (Buda and Pest banks, about 2,850 km, ten countries, a delta on the Romania–Ukraine border), but they go beyond what was asked. A is short and direct. Neither is clearly better.

Both answers correctly say the Danube flows through Budapest and into the Black Sea. A's extra details are accurate: the Buda/Pest split, a source in the Black Forest, a length of about 2,850 km through ten countries, and a delta on the Romania–Ukraine border. Still, they go beyond what was asked. B is short, correct and cited. Neither is clearly better.

B gets it right: Oxford (The Queen's College), 1973–76, a first in physics, plus accurate details about the home-built computer and the hacking ban. A never says Oxford and lists Emanuel School, which is a secondary school, as if it were his university. Its citations are also muddled, with duplicates and an unused Southampton source.

A gives the right answer clearly: Queen's College, Oxford, 1973–76, first-class physics, plus accurate details from his biographies. B never says Oxford. It also lists Emanuel School, which is a secondary school, alongside his college as if both were universities, and its sources are vague. The CERN detail in B is true but off-topic.

Both correctly name Japan and Mount Fuji. B adds accurate details (3,776 m, stratovolcano on Honshu, UNESCO site), and its sources support them. A is correct but bare, and it lists irrelevant sources (Mount Olympus, Mauna Kea). B is somewhat more useful without padding.

Both correctly identify Japan (Tokyo 1964) and Mount Fuji. A adds accurate useful details: the 3,776 m height, its location and its UNESCO status. B is correct but bare, and lists irrelevant sources such as Mount Olympus and Mauna Kea. A is slightly more informative without padding.

A is accurate but vague and generic, and it lists sources [4] and [5] that it never uses. B gives specific, accurate details: the Theses spread within weeks, the 291 editions and roughly 300,000 copies, Flugschriften pamphlets read aloud to people who couldn't read, the vernacular Bible, and the economic-history evidence. It also notes that scholars still debate the cause. B is clearly better.

A gives accurate, specific evidence: the Theses spreading within weeks, the 300,000 copies, cheap Flugschriften read aloud, the vernacular Bible and the link between print cities and Protestant adoption. It also notes that scholars still debate how much print itself caused this. B is correct but vague and generic, with little substance. Neither makes up anything that matters.

Both answers say yes and do the arithmetic correctly. B is better: its figures check out (about 541/km² on land, about 436/km² including water, about 240/km² for Germany) and it explains why the ratio varies. A's 480/km² fits neither standard measure and its sources are duplicated, though its ~2x conclusion is still roughly right.

A's numbers check out (18.1M/33,500 ≈ 540; ratios 2.25× and 1.8× are right). It also explains why the land-only and total-area figures differ, and its sources are specific. B's math holds, but its 480/km² figure for the Netherlands is not a standard number, it ignores the water-area question, and its sources are vague, with duplicates.

Both correctly give about 1.3 million by volume and a diameter of about 109 Earths. B also explains the cube scaling and adds that whole spheres pack at most about 74% of a space, giving roughly 960,000 intact Earths. That figure checks out (1.3M × 0.74 ≈ 962,000) and is supported by its sources. A is correct but thinner, and it lists source [5] without using it.

Both answers correctly give about 1.3 million Earths by volume and a 109× diameter ratio. A also shows the cube calculation and explains that solid spheres pack at about 74%, giving roughly 960,000 whole Earths. That is accurate, cited and adds real insight. B is correct but thin.

B answers directly, cites the CDC Yellow Book, and explains why: old pipes and rooftop tanks contaminate treated water. A is honest about its limits but leans on unrelated cities and gives weak, hedged advice. B's ice tip has no source, but it is minor.

Answer A gives a clear, correct "no", backed by the CDC Yellow Book. It explains why the water gets contaminated (old pipes, sinking ground, rooftop tanks) and gives practical tips. Answer B reaches roughly the right conclusion but hedges a lot, brings in irrelevant sources (Diyarbakır, Monterrey) and suggests only poorer zones are a risk, which is misleading.

Both give the right answer: you don't tip. A goes too far in calling a tip an "insult" that could offend, and it cites source [4] without using it. B is accurate and more complete. It covers service charges, otoshi and seating fees, servers handing money back, and how to say thanks instead. It also stays clear and short.

Both answers correctly say not to tip. A is accurate and more nuanced: it covers service charges, otoshi and seating charges, staff returning money, and how to say thanks. B is correct and shorter, but its claim that a tip "is seen as an insult" overstates the norm. A is more complete and more precise.

A is a thin list that omits Fushimi Inari and Arashiyama, includes Kyoto Tower, gives no two-day plan, and adds irrelevant filler. B gives an accurate plan for each day, grouped by area, with sound crowd-timing tips (Fushimi Inari is open 24 hours) and sources that fit its claims. B is clearly better.

A is better. It gives an accurate two-day plan grouped by area, with practical tips on avoiding crowds that match its sources. B is just a list with no day-by-day plan. It includes weak picks like Kyoto Tower and filler about the prefecture capital and higher learning, so it's far less useful for planning.

Answer A wrongly lists malaria prophylaxis as a vaccine. It also treats yellow fever as optional, which understates the CDC recommendation for safari areas, and it adds meningitis, which the CDC doesn't list for Kenya. Answer B is accurate: it covers the entry certificate rule, routine and situational vaccines, and malaria pills, and it says it couldn't check Kenya's Ministry of Health page.

A gets the yellow fever entry rules right, lists the CDC recommendations, separates malaria pills from vaccines, and says what it couldn't confirm. B calls malaria prophylaxis a vaccine and adds meningitis, which may not be a CDC recommendation for Kenya. B is also vague, and three citations are the same source.

A is vague and partly wrong: it suggests camping near water and washing there, which goes against Leave No Trace, and two of its sources are empty labels. B gets the legal details (Scotland, Dartmoor 2025) and the Leave No Trace guidance right. However, it invents a persona ("where I live in Scotland"), and the two-to-three-night limit is written in the Scottish code, not an unwritten rule. B is still much better.

A is accurate on Scotland, England and Wales, the 2025 Dartmoor ruling and the Leave No Trace distances, but invents a 'where I live in Scotland' claim and wrongly calls the 2–3 night rule unwritten. B is vague, suggests camping near water (against Leave No Trace), mentions restaurants, and cites junk sources ('Mind', 'Keep').

B gives practical, accurate food lists and a detailed avoid list (avocado, chocolate, salt, onion, xylitol, fruit pits) with sensible caveats. A is thin: it lists natural diet items like carrion that you wouldn't feed, mentions flour, and its avoid list is minimal. B is much more useful.

A covers safe foods and a well-sourced list of foods to avoid (bread, salt, avocado, chocolate, onion, pits, xylitol), and it says plainly that the toxic list comes from pet-bird guidance. B is accurate but thin. It describes what birds eat in nature rather than what to feed them, and its "avoid" list is brief and vague.

Answer A goes off-topic and never mentions lubrication. It cites sources about cabinet hinge installation and safety, and passes off installing a hinge as the fix for a squeak. Answer B gives the correct, standard fix: lubricate the hinge, pull the pin, clean and oil it, then tighten the screws or replace the hinge. It is clear and backed by relevant sources.

A gives accurate, practical steps: spray lubricant, pull the pin one hinge at a time, clean and oil it, then tighten screws or replace the hinge. Its sources are relevant. B uses irrelevant sources (cabinet hinge installation, child safety, door knockers) and never explains how to stop a squeak, so it is misleading and not useful.

B answers "for good" by tackling damp: humidity, ventilation and leaks. Its claims match EPA guidance on bleach, the 10 sq ft limit and 30–50% humidity. A only covers cleaning, with no prevention, and lists irrelevant sources such as injection moulding. Its bleach dilution is roughly right but it misses the core of the question.

A covers both removal and prevention, which is what "for good" needs: humidity levels, ventilation, sealant replacement and when to call a professional. Its claims are accurate and fit the EPA and Rentokil sources it cites. B only covers cleaning and says nothing about stopping the mould returning. It also leans on bleach and cites irrelevant sources, such as one on injection moulding.

B gives correct, complete steps (including dividing by a and using ±), a correct example, and notes on the edge case, and it reads well on a phone. A starts from ax²+bx+c but skips dividing by a, so the step is only valid when a=1. It also omits ± and has no inline citations, though its example is right.

A gives correct steps, including dividing by a. It also covers ± and the case with no real solutions, and its worked example is correct. B tells you to add (b/2)² to ax²+bx+c without dividing by a first, which is wrong when a≠1. B's example is correct, but its citations are not tied to its claims.

B is current and detailed, with claims backed by Apple Newsroom and trade press. Its one real error: it says the Duo "arrives next month," but its own Oct 23 launch date has passed. A is out of date (iPhone 17 family) and wrongly calls Camera Control new. Its iPhone 16 details are off-topic, and its generic Wikipedia sources don't support it.

A covers the current lineup (iPhone 18 Pro and Duo) in detail with sources, but wrongly says the Duo "arrives next month" when its own date (Oct 23) has passed. B is out of date: it calls the iPhone 17 lineup the latest, presents Camera Control as new when it came with the iPhone 16, drifts into iPhone 16 history and cites only vague sources.

B explains the smell with specific, accurate chemistry (H2S, butyric, propionic and acetic acids from Halanaerobium), the buildup of gas in the can, and how it is made. A is vague on why it smells, makes a doubtful 'deep breath' claim, and lists sources it never uses.

A is accurate and specific: it covers the process, the timing, how it's eaten, the Halanaerobium bacteria, the exact odor compounds and why the cans bulge. B is vague about the cause of the smell, never names any compounds, and gives dubious advice about taking a deep breath to knock out your sense of smell. A answers both parts much better.

A gets the basics right, but its treatment claims ("cooling blood," "ticklish areas") are garbled or made up; physicians actually prescribed more dancing. It also omits the city's response and the deaths debate. B is accurate and thorough: the response and its reversal, the Saint Vitus shrine, the disputed deaths, and both theories, all well sourced.

A is accurate and thorough: the outbreak, the city's response, how it ended, the death dispute and the causes. B is thin and misses the musicians and the shrine. Its blood-cooling and tickling claim looks taken from general dancing mania, not 1518, and its sources are vague. A is clearly better.

Both explain the Sydney–Melbourne compromise. B is accurate and fuller: it covers section 125, the 100-mile rule, Melbourne as interim seat, the 1908 site choice and Parliament's 1927 move. A is thinner and wrongly calls Sydney the "Australian colonial capital since 1788"; it was the capital of the NSW colony. A also cites sources that don't match its claims well.

A gets the Sydney–Melbourne rivalry, section 125 (inside NSW, 100+ miles from Sydney, Melbourne as interim seat), the 1908 site choice and the 1927 move right. B is thinner and misleadingly calls Sydney the 'Australian colonial capital since 1788'; it was the capital of NSW. B also lists the same source repeatedly.

B clearly explains the turbine test, disabled safety systems, xenon, the positive void coefficient and the control-rod tip flaw, with accurate details on the aftermath. A is shallow and includes a doubtful "million times" radiation claim. It also leaves out Pripyat's next-day evacuation. B is better.

A correctly explains the causes: the positive void coefficient, the control-rod tip flaw, xenon and the lack of containment. It builds on the earlier water/steam explanation. B is shallow and claims a dubious "nearly one million times" radiation rise in Europe and North America. It barely explains the causes.

Both answers correctly name Alexander Fleming, give 1928 and St Mary's, and mention the 1945 Nobel he shared with Florey and Chain. A is short and fully answers the question. B adds the date dispute and the Oxford development work. That context is accurate but not needed for this simple question, and the sources cited in each answer support its claims.

Both correctly name Alexander Fleming in 1928 at St Mary's and note the 1945 Nobel shared with Florey and Chain. A adds useful, accurate context: the date variation, how he noticed the mould, and Oxford's role in development. Its source URL is malformed, but that's a citation-format issue. B is accurate and concise but thinner.

Both correctly name Vivaldi. A says the concertos were 'written in 1725', but 1725 is the publication date. It also lists irrelevant sources. B gives the date accurately as publication (Op. 8, Amsterdam) and adds useful, correct background. Minor flaws: a slightly loose 1718–1723 range and an uncited last sentence.

Both answers correctly name Vivaldi. A adds accurate context: the 1725 Op. 8 publication, the concerto structure and the sonnets. Its 1718–1723 dating is slightly loose, and the Piazzolla/Richter line has no citation. B says the concertos were "written in 1725" when that is the publication year, and it lists irrelevant sources (Four Lions, Seasons of Love).

Both answers correctly name iron and give the Latin origin, ferrum. B also gives atomic number 26 and Group 8, which are accurate but weren't asked for. A lists six sources but cites only two of them, which is a minor problem. Both are clear and work well on a phone, and neither is clearly better.

Both answers correctly say Fe is iron, from the Latin "ferrum". A also gives atomic number 26 and Group 8, which are accurate and supported by its Britannica source. B is just as correct and complete for this simple question. A's duplicated source list is a formatting issue only. Neither is clearly better.

Answer A wrongly names China, using outdated 2023 data, though India overtook China in 2023. Answer B correctly names India, gives plausible UN estimates and the April 2023 crossover, and notes that figures are estimates because the last full census was in 2011. B is accurate, grounded and concise.

A is correct: UN estimates show India passed China in 2023, and A gives sensible figures and notes they are estimates. B wrongly names China as the largest and calls India second. That error goes to the heart of the question, and its sources probably don't back the claim as of today.

Both correctly name Bill Gates and Paul Allen and give the April 4, 1975 founding date. A's November 26, 1976 trade-name registration is accurate, and A is short and direct. B's extra context (Albuquerque, MITS/Altair, "Micro-Soft", the 1979 move) is accurate but goes beyond what was asked. Neither is clearly better.

Both answers correctly name Bill Gates and Paul Allen and give the April 4, 1975 founding date. A adds accurate context: Albuquerque, MITS and the Altair, Allen naming it "Micro-Soft", and the 1979 move. B is correct but bare; its November 1976 registration date checks out. A is slightly more useful and still short enough to read on a phone.

Both give the correct 384,400 km average. A's range of 356,400–406,700 km correctly gives the extreme values, but it lists sources it never cites. B adds miles, typical closest and farthest distances, and explains why some sources say 384,400 km and others 385,000 km. Both are accurate; B is more complete and better grounded.

Both give the correct 384,400 km. A adds accurate context: it is the semi-major axis, measured centre to centre, with typical perigee/apogee values, and it explains the 385,000 km time-averaged figure. B is correct and concise and gives the extreme range accurately, but wrongly claims the figure is quoted "consistently". A is slightly more complete and nuanced.

Both answers correctly give 206. B adds the accurate split of 80 axial and 126 appendicular bones, plus real-world variation such as sesamoid bones and extra ribs. B calls 206 "an average," which is slightly loose wording. A's figure of about 300 bones at birth is acceptable, and its point about counting conventions is valid. B is somewhat more informative.

Both correctly say 206. A adds the accurate split of 80 axial and 126 appendicular bones, plus the newborn count (~270) and the reasons adult totals vary: sesamoid bones and extra ribs or vertebrae. B is accurate too and notes counting conventions, but gives less detail. Both newborn figures (~270 and ~300) are commonly cited. A is more complete and just as clear.

Both answers correctly give 42.195 km. B also gives the mile equivalent and accurate history: the 1908 London finish at the royal box and the IAAF standard set in 1921. A is correct but thin, and its line that courses vary rests on a course-cutting source. B is somewhat more useful, though both answer the question.

Both give the correct 42.195 km. A's added history (1908 London course, the extra 385 yards, the 1921 IAAF standard) is accurate and supported by its sources, though it wasn't asked for. B is shorter, but its claim that courses vary slightly rests on a weak 'course-cutting' source. A is slightly better.

Both answers give correct masses and a ratio of about 318. A says "about 317", which truncates 317.8 rather than rounding it, a minor slip. B states the exact ratio (317.83), backs it with NASA and Wikipedia, and adds a true fact: Jupiter has about 2.5 times the mass of all other planets combined. That fact has no citation, but it is accurate. B is a bit more precise.

A gives the correct ratio of 317.83, about 318, using accurate NASA masses, and its 2.5-times-the-other-planets fact is also correct. B's masses in yottagrams are right, but it rounds the ratio down to 317 when it should be 318. Its units are hard to read, and it lists sources it never cites.

Both answers get 7.5 h right. A cites a road-trip tips page for plain arithmetic that the page probably doesn't contain, and lists unrelated sources such as the Fiat 600. B also gives the time as 7 h 30 min, says it assumes a steady 80 km/h, and notes that stops and traffic add time. It needs no sources for a simple calculation, so B is better.

Both answers get 7.5 hours right. A also converts it to 7h30m and notes that stops and traffic will lengthen the trip. B's citation [1] is unlikely to support plain arithmetic, and its other sources (Fiat 600, astronomy) are irrelevant padding, which hurts its groundedness. A is cleaner and more useful.

Both are correct. B gives the exact value (9,460,730,472,580.8 km), which checks out, and correctly explains why it is exact under the IAU definition. A's approximation is correct but less precise, it rounds the speed of light, and it lists sources it never cites. B is better.

Both answers are correct. A gives the exact IAU value (9,460,730,472,580.8 km), explains why it is exact, and still offers the rounded 9.46 trillion. B's approximation of 9.46 × 10¹² km and the speed it uses are accurate, but it gives less detail. A is clear and fully supported by its sources, so it is better.

A is accurate but thin, and its page count of 240 to 272 is fuzzy. B is far more complete: Yale MS 408, the radiocarbon date, the sections, owners and theories. Its one mistake is calling Rudolf II the earliest confirmed owner; that was Georg Baresch. On balance B is more informative and still well grounded.

A is accurate and thorough: MS 408, the 1912 purchase from Frascati, the 1404–1438 carbon date, its sections, owners, the 1969 gift and theories. Calling Rudolf II the "earliest confirmed owner" is disputed. B is correct but thin. Its 240–272 page figure is muddled and its sources are vague and duplicated.

A is accurate but thin: 1816, Tambora, crop failures, riots. "Coldest on record" overstates it, and its sources repeat. B covers the cause in depth (VEI 7), effects on several continents, the death toll and Frankenstein. Its one slip is minor: Albany snow is often dated June 6, not June 8. B is better.

A is accurate and specific: Tambora's eruption dated 5–10 April 1815, plus correct details on the June snow, oat prices, Irish typhus, coloured snow, Yangtze floods and Frankenstein. B is accurate but thin. It omits cultural effects and Asia, and 'coldest summer on record' may overstate. A covers more and is better grounded.

A wrongly says Mpemba first described the effect, when Aristotle, Bacon and Descartes did so centuries earlier. It presents causes as settled, skips the dispute, and lists an unrelated Bouba/kiki source. B is accurate: it covers the 1969 paper, earlier observers, the dispute, Burridge & Linden, and the 2012 RSC prize. It also flags uncited background knowledge.

A is accurate (the 1963/1969 dates, Osborne, Burridge & Linden 2016, the RSC prize), covers the dispute and the competing explanations, and flags its uncited background knowledge. B is correct on the basics but leaves out that the effect's existence is disputed, oversimplifies the causes and lists an unrelated Bouba/kiki source.

Both get the core facts right (1932, Campion, Meredith, Lewis guns, 2 Nov–10 Dec). A is thin: it leaves out the drought, the ~20,000 emus, the withdrawal and the kill count, and it cites an unrelated "EMU Australia" source. B is fuller and accurate. Its bounty figure (284,704) may be slightly off from the commonly cited figure, which is a minor issue. B is better.

A is accurate and fuller: drought, about 20,000 emus, veteran farmers, two Lewis guns, a pull-out and a return, 986 kills, and bounties. B is correct in outline but thin, with no cause or numbers. It wrongly treats "machine guns and Lewis guns" as different weapons and names the unit "7th Heavy Artillery" (it was the 7th Heavy Battery). It also cites an unrelated boot brand.

Both answers are accurate.
